items.excerpt: Comparison of Paradigms The formalization of Context Engineering highlights its fundamental distinctions from traditional prompt engineering. The following table summarizes the key differences. In summary, Context Engineering provides the formal, systematic framework required to build, understand, and optimize the sophisticated, context-aware AI systems that are coming to define the future of the field.
items.statement: Unlike prompt engineering, which relies primarily on manual instructions, context engineering utilizes algorithmic pipelines to dynamically select and format input data for large language models.
items.label: NOT_FOUND
items.why: The statement describes specific operational differences between prompt and context engineering that are not mentioned in the short excerpt.

items.excerpt: We analyze the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. We find that performance can degrade significantly when changing the position of relevant information, indicating that current language models do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts.
items.statement: The accuracy of modern language models on multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval shifts substantially based on where the crucial data is located in the input.
items.label: SUPPORTED
items.why: I paraphrased the finding that language model accuracy on key-value retrieval and multi-document question answering degrades significantly when the location of relevant information is changed.
items.verification: grep -Fzo 'We analyze the performance of language models on two' combined.txt  # excerpt present verbatim, 1 hit (may straddle a line wrap; -z spans it)

items.excerpt: Main context consists of the LLM prompt tokens— anything in main context is considered in-context and can be accessed by the LLM processor during inference. External context refers to any information that is held outside of the LLMs fixed context window.
items.statement: Data residing in the main context is available for immediate retrieval during model processing, while external context comprises data positioned beyond this defined boundary.
items.label: SUPPORTED
items.why: The statement paraphrases the definitions of main and external context, confirming that the former is accessible during processing while the latter lies outside the memory limits.
items.verification: grep -Fzo 'Main context consists of the LLM prompt tokens— anything' combined.txt  # excerpt present verbatim, 1 hit (may straddle a line wrap; -z spans it)

items.excerpt: Monolithic rewriting of context by an LLM can collapse it into shorter, less informative summaries, leading to sharp performance drops. Context Collapse In a case study on the AppWorld benchmark (Trivedi et al., 2024), we observe a phenomenon we call context collapse, which arises when an LLM is tasked with fully rewriting the accumulated context at each adaptation step.
items.statement: During sequential system adjustments, a language model that completely regenerates its gathered background information risks experiencing context collapse, which severely degrades its final results.
items.label: SUPPORTED
items.why: The statement paraphrases how fully rewriting accumulated context during adaptation steps can cause context collapse, leading to information loss and degraded performance.

items.excerpt: However, their long-term memory capabilities in sustained interactions remain underexplored. We introduce L ONG M EM E VAL, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate five core long-term memory abilities of chat assistants: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. With 500 meticulously curated questions embedded within freely scalable user-assistant chat histories, L ONG M EM E VAL presents a significant challenge to existing long-term memory systems, with commercial chat assistants and long-context LLMs showing a 30% accuracy drop on memorizing information across sustained interactions.
items.statement: When tested on LongMemEval, proprietary chatbots and extended-context language models exhibit a 30% performance reduction when recalling facts over extended dialogues.
items.label: SUPPORTED
items.why: I paraphrased the excerpt's finding regarding the thirty percent decrease in the accuracy of chat assistants and models over long conversations.

items.excerpt: As observed in [KMH+ 20], language modeling performance follows a power-law when making efficient use of training compute. After extending this trend by two more orders of magnitude, we observe only a slight (if any) departure from the power-law. One might worry that these improvements in cross-entropy loss come only from modeling spurious details of our training corpus. However, we will see in the following sections that improvements in cross-entropy loss lead to consistent performance gains across a broad spectrum of natural language tasks.

items.excerpt: Similarly, Gemini 1.5 Flash achieves almost perfect recall across all three modalities up to 2M tokens, yielding 100% recall on text, 99.8% on video and 99.1% on audio. items.excerpt: Gemini 1.5 models achieve near-perfect recall on long-context retrieval tasks across modalities, improve the state-of-the-art in long-document QA, long-video QA and long-context ASR, and match or surpass Gemini 1.0 Ultra’s state-of-the-art performance across a broad set of benchmarks. Studying the limits of Gemini 1.5’s long-context ability, we find continued improvement in next-token prediction and near-perfect retrieval (>99%) up to at least 10M tokens, a generational leap over existing models such as Claude 3.0 (200k) and GPT-4 Turbo (128k).
